Analysis

Do captains get it right?

Hussain at the Gabba, Ponting at Edgbaston, Rohit at the Oval: we replayed three famous toss calls to see what they really cost, and what the XI picked around them cost.

S
Staff The Grass Bank™ Analysis
November 12, 2026

Introduction

The toss takes a minute. The argument about it can last twenty years.

At the Gabba in November 2002, Nasser Hussain won the toss and put Australia in. Simon Jones tore his knee ligaments on the sandy outfield that first morning. Matthew Hayden and Ricky Ponting added 272, Australia closed the day on 364 for 2, and England lost by 384 runs. Hussain has been asked about that call ever since.

Three years later at Edgbaston, Glenn McGrath stepped on a stray ball in the warm-up and was ruled out an hour before the start. Ponting won the toss and bowled anyway. England made 407 on the first day. Australia lost by two runs, the narrowest margin in Ashes history, and Shane Warne never let him forget it.

At the Oval in June 2023, in the World Test Championship final, Rohit Sharma won the toss and bowled. R Ashwin, the No. 1 bowler in the world, was left out. I was at the ground. It was bright and sunny on the first day, and by lunch I was sure how it would end. Travis Head and Steve Smith took Australia to 327 for 3 by stumps; they made 469. In the fourth innings Nathan Lyon took 4 for 41: the spell India had left on the bench. India lost by 209 runs.

Every cricket fan has a list like this. Were these the wrong calls, or just calls that went wrong? And how often do captains get the toss right at all?

How captains decide

Captains decide mostly on where they are playing and what their own attack looks like. The opposition matters less than the commentary suggests.

We looked at 1,799 Tests since 1976 where we know who won the toss and what they chose. For each, we measured how much of each side's bowling was likely to come from spinners, and where the match was played: Asia, the seaming countries (England, New Zealand, South Africa, Ireland), or elsewhere.

The opposition's attack comes into it, but as a second thought. Captains do sometimes bowl first to keep their batters away from a great new-ball pair on a fresh pitch: a defensive toss. But in the data, the other side's spin moves the decision only at the margins.

What the decision trades away

The choice at the toss often comes with a choice at selection. A captain who expects to bowl first on a green pitch picks an extra seamer, and the spinner is the man who sits out. That is what happened at the Oval. It gives up the fourth innings, when the pitch is worn and a spinner is at his most dangerous.

We expected that cost to show up in results. It mostly didn't. Captains who won the toss and bowled first without a frontline spinner won 48% of those Tests, when our model, working only from the two XIs, expected 34%. Captains who bowled first with a spinner did 4 points better than expected. Those who batted first did about as well as expected.

The likeliest reason is the simplest one. A captain who bowls first has usually seen something: grass, cloud, a damp surface. Our model knows only the players. When the captain's read is right, the pace bowlers take their wickets early, and nobody misses the spinner in the fourth innings because the game is already won. In the Tests since 2006 where the captain chose to bowl, pace bowlers took about 11% more wickets than usual in the first innings, and the edge faded as the match went on.

Did they get it right?

We replayed all three Tests in our match simulator, 3,000 times each, with the toss as it was called and with the call reversed. Each replay uses only what was known before the first ball: players rated on their records up to that Test, and a model learned only from Tests already finished. The Oval is simulated ball by ball; the two older Tests, wicket by wicket.

The replays judge each call on the players alone: the two XIs, the ground and who bats first. They cannot see the pitch or the sky on the day, so they cannot say whether a captain read the conditions right. What they can say is what the call was worth, given the two sides.

The toss

The side's chance of winning, from 3,000 replays of each Test. Every replay number in this article comes from the same run, so the figures can be compared with each other; each is accurate to within about a point.

Hussain's call, the most mocked toss in Ashes history, barely moved the needle. England were six-to-one against whatever he did. Australia had Hayden, Ponting, Warne and McGrath, and England lost Jones before lunch. The call looked terrible by the evening, but it was not what lost the Test.

Ponting's call cost nothing either. With McGrath gone, Australia were around 40% whichever way he went, and they lost by two runs: a match that could have gone either way, and nearly did.

Rohit's is the one that moves. On the players alone, batting first was worth about 7 points to India.

Most of those 7 points come from one thing: which side's spinner gets the worn pitch. Bat first, and Lyon bowls on a fresh surface while Jadeja gets the fourth innings. When we replayed the final with spinners made equally dangerous in every innings, batting first was worth only 4 points. Lyon himself is not the special case. From 2011 to the final, his wickets cost 28.5 in the third and fourth innings, about the same as other spinners. Where he beat them was early, on fresh pitches: 33.7 to their 39.0.

The XI

The toss decision at the Oval came with a selection decision, and it was really two questions: one spinner or two, and if one, which one. India picked four seamers and one spinner, Ravindra Jadeja, and left out Ashwin, the number 1 bowler in the world at that time. So we replayed the final both ways: with Ashwin alongside Jadeja, in place of Umesh Yadav and then of Shardul Thakur, and with Ashwin instead of Jadeja.

India's chance of winning the final.

India's best final had Ashwin in the side. On the players alone, the best call was to bat first with Ashwin in for Umesh: 34% against the 27% India actually took into the match. That is the largest gap of the three Tests.

With Ashwin in for Umesh Yadav, India's chances improve by 7%

Had India batted first with Ashwin in for Jadeja, their chance would have risen from 24% to 29%. But all of that comes from batting first: with Jadeja kept, batting first gives 31%. Swapping one spinner for the other adds nothing, because India still have only one spinner and lose Jadeja's batting at No. 6. What adds to the toss is a second spinner, Ashwin alongside Jadeja in place of a seamer: 3 to 5 points more.

The record in England

The replays rate players on their whole careers. They do not know that Ashwin had bowled far better in England than Jadeja had.

Outside Asia as a whole there was nothing between them: both averaged about 36 with the ball. In England, Ashwin's wickets cost 18 runs fewer.

So we replayed the final again, with both spinners' bowling rated on their record in England instead of their whole careers.

Every number falls, because both men had bowled worse in England than over their careers, Jadeja much worse. But the order changes. On English figures, Ashwin for Jadeja is no longer a wash: it is worth a point bowling first and 4 batting first, about as much as Ashwin for a seamer. The toss still matters most: batting first is worth 4 to 7 points with any of these XIs.

If India were to play only one spinner, by their records in England it should have been Ashwin. A few points is a small margin, but this is a game of small margins, and a captain's job is to take every one he can.

Two cautions. The samples are small, 18 and 23 wickets. And only India's two spinners were re-rated; Lyon and the seamers on both sides kept their career figures.

Rohit and the tree

By the record of other captains, set out in our decision tree for the toss, Rohit's call was neither right nor wrong. Visiting toss winners in England who bowled first won 33% and lost 44%; those who batted won 29% and lost 43%. It has made little difference which way they go.

But the tree describes captains on average, across hundreds of pitches. The replay of this match, with these two XIs, is more specific: on the players alone, batting first was worth 7 points to India. The tree says the call was defensible; the replay says it was costly. And the tree cannot see the XI that came with the call, which cost India another 3 to 5 points.

Conclusion

Captains get it right most of the time. In Asia they bat; away from Asia with a pace attack they bowl; and when they choose to bowl, they win more often than the players alone would suggest. The toss is not a lottery they keep losing. It is a judgement they mostly make well.

The famous mistakes are rarer than the arguments about them. Hussain's call at the Gabba is remembered as the worst toss in Ashes history, but England were beaten before the coin went up. Ponting's at Edgbaston cost Australia almost nothing; two runs did.

Rohit's call at the Oval was different, because it was really two decisions. On the players alone, bowling first on a bright, sunny first morning gave up about 7 points. Leaving out the world's No. 1 bowler to do it gave up about 4 more. Together they took India from 35% to 24%, from about one chance in three to one in four, and Nathan Lyon's 4 for 41 on the last day showed what the bench had cost.

So the toss is seldom where Tests are lost. But when it is, it rarely comes alone: at the Oval, the call cost India about 7 points and the XI picked around it about 4 more.

What has worked for toss winners in each country, home or away, is set out in the companion piece, A decision tree for the toss.
